paragraphs.text: וַיְהִי֙ כִּֽי־זָקֵ֣ן יִצְחָ֔ק וַתִּכְהֶ֥יןָ עֵינָ֖יו מֵרְאֹ֑ת וַיִּקְרָ֞א אֶת־עֵשָׂ֣ו ׀ בְּנ֣וֹ הַגָּדֹ֗ל וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ בְּנִ֔י וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֵלָ֖יו הִנֵּֽנִי׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when Yitzchaq was old, and his eyes were dim from seeing, that he called Esav his elder son, and said to him, My son. And he said to him, Here am I.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-tikheina eynav me-r'ot* — "his eyes were dim from seeing." The verb *kahah* (קָהָה) covers a semantic range from "be dim, dull, weak" to "fail entirely" (BDB 462; HALOT s.v.). The Hebrew construction with privative-*min* (*me-r'ot*, "from seeing") is preserved here rather than smoothed to the ASV/KJV result-clause "so that he could not see" or NJPS's "too dim to see"; the literal preposition surfaces the lexical core.

The formula is one of the Hebrew Bible's narrative-trigger conventions for transferred-perception or transferred-authority episodes. Compare Mosheh at Deut 34:7 (negated — *lo-khahatah eyno*, "his eye had not dimmed," marking the *absence* of the trigger), Eli at 1 Sam 3:2, Achiyah at 1 Kgs 14:4: in each case patriarchal-blindness sets up a deception, a misidentification, or a generational hand-off. Yitzchaq's blindness is the mechanism that makes the chapter's blessing-deception possible. The glossary entry [kahah-eynayim-patriarchal-blindness-narrative-trigger](#kahah-eynayim-patriarchal-blindness-narrative-trigger) cross-references the cluster.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הִנֵּה־נָ֖א זָקַ֑נְתִּי לֹ֥א יָדַ֖עְתִּי י֥וֹם מוֹתִֽי׃

i18n.en: And he said, Behold now, I am old; I do not know the day of my death.

paragraphs.text: וְעַתָּה֙ שָׂא־נָ֣א כֵלֶ֔יךָ תֶּלְיְךָ֖ וְקַשְׁתֶּ֑ךָ וְצֵא֙ הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה וְצ֥וּדָה לִּ֖י צידה [צָֽיִד׃]

i18n.en: Now therefore take, I pray you, your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field, and hunt me venison.

paragraphs.text: וַעֲשֵׂה־לִ֨י מַטְעַמִּ֜ים כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָהַ֛בְתִּי וְהָבִ֥יאָה לִּ֖י וְאֹכֵ֑לָה בַּעֲב֛וּר תְּבָרֶכְךָ֥ נַפְשִׁ֖י בְּטֶ֥רֶם אָמֽוּת׃

i18n.en: And make me savory food, such as I love, and bring it to me, that I may eat; that my nefesh may bless you before I die.

paragraphs.commentary:
Two lexically loaded terms organize the chapter's blessing-mechanism. *Matamim* (מַטְעַמִּים), "savory food," is from the root *ta'am* (טעם, "taste"); BDB 381, HALOT s.v. KJV/ASV give "savoury meat"; NJPS smooths to "a dish." The term appears six times in this chapter (vv 4, 7, 9, 14, 17, 31) and only here in the Torah — a chapter-specific fixed phrase that names the blessing-transfer meal. See [matamim-savory-food-blessing-meal](#matamim-savory-food-blessing-meal).

*Ba'avur t-varekhekha nafshi* — "that my nefesh may bless you" — is the chapter's organizing-formula for what a blessing actually is. The construction recurs at vv 19, 25, 31: in each case the *nefesh* (not the man, not the mouth, not the hand) is the grammatical subject of the verb "bless." KJV's "my soul" carries post-Hellenistic baggage the Hebrew does not have; NJPS's "give you my innermost blessing" smooths the syntactic point away. Following Wolff (*Anthropology of the Old Testament*) and the project's prior *nefesh*-cluster entries, *nefesh* here is the patriarchal vital-self — the seat of the appetites and of the life-force whose transmission *is* the blessing. The translation transliterates per project convention. See [nefesh-blessing-transfer](#nefesh-blessing-transfer).

paragraphs.text: וְרִבְקָ֣ה שֹׁמַ֔עַת בְּדַבֵּ֣ר יִצְחָ֔ק אֶל־עֵשָׂ֖ו בְּנ֑וֹ וַיֵּ֤לֶךְ עֵשָׂו֙ הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה לָצ֥וּד צַ֖יִד לְהָבִֽיא׃

paragraphs.text: וְרִבְקָה֙ אָֽמְרָ֔ה אֶל־יַעֲקֹ֥ב בְּנָ֖הּ לֵאמֹ֑ר הִנֵּ֤ה שָׁמַ֙עְתִּי֙ אֶת־אָבִ֔יךָ מְדַבֵּ֛ר אֶל־עֵשָׂ֥ו אָחִ֖יךָ לֵאמֹֽר׃

paragraphs.text: הָבִ֨יאָה לִּ֥י צַ֛יִד וַעֲשֵׂה־לִ֥י מַטְעַמִּ֖ים וְאֹכֵ֑לָה וַאֲבָרֶכְכָ֛ה לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י מוֹתִֽי׃

paragraphs.text: וְעַתָּ֥ה בְנִ֖י שְׁמַ֣ע בְּקֹלִ֑י לַאֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲנִ֖י מְצַוָּ֥ה אֹתָֽךְ׃

i18n.en: Now therefore, my son, obey my voice in that which I command you.

paragraphs.text: לֶךְ־נָא֙ אֶל־הַצֹּ֔אן וְקַֽח־לִ֣י מִשָּׁ֗ם שְׁנֵ֛י גְּדָיֵ֥י עִזִּ֖ים טֹבִ֑ים וְאֶֽעֱשֶׂ֨ה אֹתָ֧ם מַטְעַמִּ֛ים לְאָבִ֖יךָ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָהֵֽב׃

i18n.en: Go now to the flock, and bring me from there two good kids of the goats; and I will make of them savory food for your father, such as he loves.

paragraphs.text: וְהֵבֵאתָ֥ לְאָבִ֖יךָ וְאָכָ֑ל בַּעֲבֻ֛ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר יְבָרֶכְךָ֖ לִפְנֵ֥י מוֹתֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And you shall bring it to your father, that he may eat, so that he may bless you before his death.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יַעֲקֹ֔ב אֶל־רִבְקָ֖ה אִמּ֑וֹ הֵ֣ן עֵשָׂ֤ו אָחִי֙ אִ֣ישׁ שָׂעִ֔ר וְאָנֹכִ֖י אִ֥ישׁ חָלָֽק׃

paragraphs.text: אוּלַ֤י יְמֻשֵּׁ֙נִי֙ אָבִ֔י וְהָיִ֥יתִי בְעֵינָ֖יו כִּמְתַעְתֵּ֑עַ וְהֵבֵאתִ֥י עָלַ֛י קְלָלָ֖ה וְלֹ֥א בְרָכָֽה׃

i18n.en: Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall be in his eyes as a deceiver; and I shall bring a curse upon myself, and not a blessing.

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ אִמּ֔וֹ עָלַ֥י קִלְלָתְךָ֖ בְּנִ֑י אַ֛ךְ שְׁמַ֥ע בְּקֹלִ֖י וְלֵ֥ךְ קַֽח־לִֽי׃

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּ֙לֶךְ֙ וַיִּקַּ֔ח וַיָּבֵ֖א לְאִמּ֑וֹ וַתַּ֤עַשׂ אִמּוֹ֙ מַטְעַמִּ֔ים כַּאֲשֶׁ֖ר אָהֵ֥ב אָבִֽיו׃

i18n.en: And he went, and took, and brought them to his mother; and his mother made savory food, such as his father loved.

paragraphs.text: וַתִּקַּ֣ח רִ֠בְקָה אֶת־בִּגְדֵ֨י עֵשָׂ֜ו בְּנָ֤הּ הַגָּדֹל֙ הַחֲמֻדֹ֔ת אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתָּ֖הּ בַּבָּ֑יִת וַתַּלְבֵּ֥שׁ אֶֽת־יַעֲקֹ֖ב בְּנָ֥הּ הַקָּטָֽן׃

paragraphs.text: וְאֵ֗ת עֹרֹת֙ גְּדָיֵ֣י הָֽעִזִּ֔ים הִלְבִּ֖ישָׁה עַל־יָדָ֑יו וְעַ֖ל חֶלְקַ֥ת צַוָּארָֽיו׃

paragraphs.text: וַתִּתֵּ֧ן אֶת־הַמַּטְעַמִּ֛ים וְאֶת־הַלֶּ֖חֶם אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֑תָה בְּיַ֖ד יַעֲקֹ֥ב בְּנָֽהּ׃

i18n.en: And she gave the savory food and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of Ya'aqov her son.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֥א אֶל־אָבִ֖יו וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אָבִ֑י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הִנֶּ֔נִּי מִ֥י אַתָּ֖ה בְּנִֽי׃

i18n.en: And he came to his father, and said, My father. And he said, Here am I; who are you, my son?

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יַעֲקֹ֜ב אֶל־אָבִ֗יו אָנֹכִי֙ עֵשָׂ֣ו בְּכֹרֶ֔ךָ עָשִׂ֕יתִי כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּ֖רְתָּ אֵלָ֑י קֽוּם־נָ֣א שְׁבָ֗ה וְאָכְלָה֙ מִצֵּידִ֔י בַּעֲב֖וּר תְּבָרֲכַ֥נִּי נַפְשֶֽׁךָ׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov said to his father, I am Esav your firstborn; I have done as you spoke to me. Arise, I pray you, sit and eat of my venison, that your nefesh may bless me.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יִצְחָק֙ אֶל־בְּנ֔וֹ מַה־זֶּ֛ה מִהַ֥רְתָּ לִמְצֹ֖א בְּנִ֑י וַיֹּ֕אמֶר כִּ֥י הִקְרָ֛ה יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ לְפָנָֽי׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq said to his son, How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son? And he said, Because YHWH your Elohim caused it to come to me.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יִצְחָק֙ אֶֽל־יַעֲקֹ֔ב גְּשָׁה־נָּ֥א וַאֲמֻֽשְׁךָ֖ בְּנִ֑י הַֽאַתָּ֥ה זֶ֛ה בְּנִ֥י עֵשָׂ֖ו אִם־לֹֽא׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq said to Ya'aqov, Come near, I pray you, that I may feel you, my son, whether you are really my son Esav or not.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּגַּ֧שׁ יַעֲקֹ֛ב אֶל־יִצְחָ֥ק אָבִ֖יו וַיְמֻשֵּׁ֑הוּ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הַקֹּל֙ ק֣וֹל יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְהַיָּדַ֖יִם יְדֵ֥י עֵשָֽׂו׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov came near to Yitzchaq his father; and he felt him, and said, The voice is the voice of Ya'aqov, but the hands are the hands of Esav.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Ha-qol qol Ya'aqov v-ha-yadayim y'dei Esav* — "the voice is the voice of Ya'aqov, but the hands are the hands of Esav." The verse is the chapter's narrative-rhetorical fulcrum and one of the Hebrew Bible's most-cited chiastic doublets. The two-clause structure with definite article on each subject and construct-state on each predicate (*ha-qol qol-X / ha-yadayim y'dei-Y*) is editorially marked; the translation preserves the article-construct repetition rather than smoothing to "this is Jacob's voice, but these are Esau's hands." ASV is the baseline; Alter (*The Five Books of Moses*) reads the doubling as deliberate verbal mirroring of the chapter's identity-confusion.

The rabbinic reception is dense. *Genesis Rabbah* 65:20 reads the *qol* as Torah-study and the *yadayim* as Esav-violence — a hermeneutic that recurs in patristic, medieval Jewish, and contemporary homiletic exegesis. The clause is also the verse from which Yitzchaq is conventionally said to have "sensed but not acted," reading the contradiction without resolving it — a feature the narrative exploits when it has him bless Ya'aqov anyway at v 23.

The Wheel of Heaven lens neither sharpens nor blunts the irony here; the chiastic-doublet is a literary feature of the Hebrew, and the translation's job is to preserve it rather than rewrite it. See [ha-qol-qol-yaakov-deception-formula](#ha-qol-qol-yaakov-deception-formula).

paragraphs.text: וְלֹ֣א הִכִּיר֔וֹ כִּֽי־הָי֣וּ יָדָ֗יו כִּידֵ֛י עֵשָׂ֥ו אָחִ֖יו שְׂעִרֹ֑ת וַֽיְבָרְכֵֽהוּ׃

i18n.en: And he did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy, as his brother Esav's hands; so he blessed him.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר אַתָּ֥ה זֶ֖ה בְּנִ֣י עֵשָׂ֑ו וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אָֽנִי׃

i18n.en: And he said, Are you really my son Esav? And he said, I am.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הַגִּ֤שָׁה לִּי֙ וְאֹֽכְלָה֙ מִצֵּ֣יד בְּנִ֔י לְמַ֥עַן תְּבָֽרֶכְךָ֖ נַפְשִׁ֑י וַיַּגֶּשׁ־לוֹ֙ וַיֹּאכַ֔ל וַיָּ֧בֵא ל֦וֹ יַ֖יִן וַיֵּֽשְׁתְּ׃

i18n.en: And he said, Bring it near to me, and I will eat of my son's venison, that my nefesh may bless you. And he brought it near to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֵלָ֖יו יִצְחָ֣ק אָבִ֑יו גְּשָׁה־נָּ֥א וּשְׁקָה־לִּ֖י בְּנִֽי׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq his father said to him, Come near now, and kiss me, my son.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּגַּשׁ֙ וַיִּשַּׁק־ל֔וֹ וַיָּ֛רַח אֶת־רֵ֥יחַ בְּגָדָ֖יו וַֽיְבָרֲכֵ֑הוּ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר רְאֵה֙ רֵ֣יחַ בְּנִ֔י כְּרֵ֣יחַ שָׂדֶ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בֵּרֲכ֖וֹ יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: And he came near, and kissed him; and he smelled the smell of his garments, and blessed him, and said, See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which YHWH has blessed.

paragraphs.text: וְיִֽתֶּן־לְךָ֙ הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים מִטַּל֙ הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וּמִשְׁמַנֵּ֖י הָאָ֑רֶץ וְרֹ֥ב דָּגָ֖ן וְתִירֹֽשׁ׃

i18n.en: And may the Elohim give you of the dew of the skies, and of the fatness of the land, and abundance of grain and new wine.

paragraphs.commentary:
The blessing-formula proper. *Mi-tal ha-shamayim u-mi-shemanei ha-aretz* — "of the dew of the skies and of the fatness of the land." The *mi-* preposition is partitive here, fixed by the parallel construction with *v-rov dagan v-tirosh* ("and abundance of grain and new wine") which is unambiguously partitive in sense. The same preposition is famously ambiguous at vv 39–40 where Yitzchaq counter-blesses Esav with formally near-identical wording — the contrast between definite-partitive at v 28 and ambiguous-*mi-* at v 39 is editorially load-bearing (see commentary at v 39).

*Dagan v-tirosh* — "grain and new wine" — is one of the canonical agricultural-blessing word-pairs of the corpus (Deut 7:13, 11:14, 28:51; Hos 2:10; Joel 1:10). *Tirosh* is specifically the new wine / must (HALOT 1727), not aged *yayin*.

The articulated *ha-Elohim* — "the Elohim" — is preserved per project convention against KJV/ASV's flat "God." The article in the Hebrew is real: Yitzchaq's blessing addresses *ha-Elohim* (the Elohim, plural collective with article), distinct from v 20's unarticulated *YHWH Eloheikha*. See [tal-shamayim-shemanei-aretz-blessing-formula](#tal-shamayim-shemanei-aretz-blessing-formula) and the standing [elohim-as-translation](#elohim-as-translation) entry.

paragraphs.text: יַֽעַבְד֣וּךָ עַמִּ֗ים וישתחו [וְיִֽשְׁתַּחֲו֤וּ] לְךָ֙ לְאֻמִּ֔ים הֱוֵ֤ה גְבִיר֙ לְאַחֶ֔יךָ וְיִשְׁתַּחֲוּ֥וּ לְךָ֖ בְּנֵ֣י אִמֶּ֑ךָ אֹרְרֶ֣יךָ אָר֔וּר וּֽמְבָרֲכֶ֖יךָ בָּרֽוּךְ׃

i18n.en: Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you; be lord over your brothers, and let your mother's sons bow down to you. Those who curse you, cursed; and those who bless you, blessed.

paragraphs.commentary:
Two interlocking blessing-formulas. *Ya'avdukha amim v-yishtachavu lekha le'umim* — "let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you." The *amim/le'umim* pair is a fixed-pair in Hebrew Bible blessing-and-oracle contexts (Gen 25:23, *shnei goyim/shnei le'umim*; Num 24:7; Isa 17:12–13; Ps 47:4); a *qere* at *yishtachavu* supplies the standard hishtaphel form against the defective *ketiv yishtachu*. The clause assigns Ya'aqov the peoples-subjugation half of the patriarchal-blessing chain.

*Orerekha arur u-m'varakhekha barukh* — "those who curse you, cursed; and those who bless you, blessed." This is an explicit reverse-echo of the curse-blessing-protection clause first issued to Avraham at Gen 12:3 (*u-m'varakhekha avarekha u-m'qallelekha a'or*). The Gen 12:3 form was the direct YHWH-theophany to Avraham; the Gen 27:29 form transmits the same clause through Yitzchaq to Ya'aqov — a transfer that ratifies the Avrahamic-blessing-chain (Avraham → Yitzchaq → Ya'aqov) one generation further. Note that v 29 uses the curse-blessing-protection clause *only*, without the universal-blessing *nivrakhu bekha* niphal/hithpael clause that follows it at Gen 12:3; the existing [nivrakhu-bekha-niphal-hithpael](#nivrakhu-bekha-niphal-hithpael) entry covers the universal-blessing clause, while [cursed-cursers-blessed-blessers-echo](#cursed-cursers-blessed-blessers-echo) covers the protection clause and its transmission to Ya'aqov here.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֗י כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר כִּלָּ֣ה יִצְחָק֮ לְבָרֵ֣ךְ אֶֽת־יַעֲקֹב֒ וַיְהִ֗י אַ֣ךְ יָצֹ֤א יָצָא֙ יַעֲקֹ֔ב מֵאֵ֥ת פְּנֵ֖י יִצְחָ֣ק אָבִ֑יו וְעֵשָׂ֣ו אָחִ֔יו בָּ֖א מִצֵּידֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, as soon as Yitzchaq had finished blessing Ya'aqov, and Ya'aqov was just gone out from before Yitzchaq his father, that Esav his brother came in from his hunting.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֤עַשׂ גַּם־הוּא֙ מַטְעַמִּ֔ים וַיָּבֵ֖א לְאָבִ֑יו וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְאָבִ֗יו יָקֻ֤ם אָבִי֙ וְיֹאכַל֙ מִצֵּ֣יד בְּנ֔וֹ בַּעֲב֖וּר תְּבָרֲכַ֥נִּי נַפְשֶֽׁךָ׃

i18n.en: And he also made savory food, and brought it to his father; and he said to his father, Let my father arise, and eat of his son's venison, that your nefesh may bless me.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֛וֹ יִצְחָ֥ק אָבִ֖יו מִי־אָ֑תָּה וַיֹּ֕אמֶר אֲנִ֛י בִּנְךָ֥ בְכֹֽרְךָ֖ עֵשָֽׂו׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq his father said to him, Who are you? And he said, I am your son, your firstborn, Esav.

paragraphs.text: וַיֶּחֱרַ֨ד יִצְחָ֣ק חֲרָדָה֮ גְּדֹלָ֣ה עַד־מְאֹד֒ וַיֹּ֡אמֶר מִֽי־אֵפ֡וֹא ה֣וּא הַצָּֽד־צַיִד֩ וַיָּ֨בֵא לִ֜י וָאֹכַ֥ל מִכֹּ֛ל בְּטֶ֥רֶם תָּב֖וֹא וָאֲבָרֲכֵ֑הוּ גַּם־בָּר֖וּךְ יִהְיֶֽה׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq trembled a great trembling exceedingly, and said, Who then is he who has hunted venison, and brought it to me, and I ate of all before you came, and I blessed him? Indeed, he shall be blessed.

paragraphs.commentary:
Two clauses, both editorially load-bearing.

*Va-yecherad Yitzchaq charadah gedolah ad-me'od* — "and Yitzchaq trembled a great trembling exceedingly." The construction is a Hebrew cognate-accusative (verb + noun from the same root) intensified by the adjective *gedolah* and the marker *ad-me'od* — three intensifiers stacked on a single emotional event. The *charad/charadah* root names the intense-fear/agitation lexical cluster (Exod 19:16 of Sinai's *charad* at the theophany; Isa 32:11; Ezek 26:18); the deployment here is the strongest narrative-emotion-marking in the patriarchal cycle. The translation preserves the cognate-accusative literally rather than ASV's smoothed "trembled very exceedingly." See [va-yecherad-charadah-trembling-formula](#va-yecherad-charadah-trembling-formula).

*Gam-barukh yihye* — "indeed, he shall be blessed." The clause is the blessing-irrevocability-declaration: once pronounced, the patriarchal blessing cannot be revoked even when extracted by deception. The reading is the source-text for the rabbinic and medieval doctrine of blessing-irrevocability and for the Heb 12:17 *topon metanoias ouk heuren* reception ("Esau found no place for repentance, though he sought it diligently with tears"). Yitzchaq's recognition of the deception does not undo the words; the blessing once spoken belongs to whomever received it. The Wheel of Heaven lens reads the clause not theologically but performatively — a blessing is a transfer of *nefesh* (see v 4 commentary), and what is transferred cannot be un-transferred.

paragraphs.text: כִּשְׁמֹ֤עַ עֵשָׂו֙ אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֣י אָבִ֔יו וַיִּצְעַ֣ק צְעָקָ֔ה גְּדֹלָ֥ה וּמָרָ֖ה עַד־מְאֹ֑ד וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְאָבִ֔יו בָּרֲכֵ֥נִי גַם־אָ֖נִי אָבִֽי׃

i18n.en: When Esav heard the words of his father, he cried out a great and bitter cry exceedingly, and said to his father, Bless me, even me also, my father.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yitz'aq tza'aqah gedolah u-marah ad-me'od* — "he cried out a great and bitter cry exceedingly." Another cognate-accusative (*tza'aq tza'aqah*), now doubled by the adjective-pair *gedolah u-marah* (great and bitter) and the intensifier *ad-me'od*. The bitter-cry formula functions as a marker of irreversible-loss in the corpus's narrative-emotional repertoire.

The phrase recurs cross-corpus most famously at Esth 4:1 of Mordecai upon learning of the destruction-decree: *va-yiz'aq ze'aqah gedolah u-marah ad-me'od* — a near-verbatim echo widely treated in the literary-critical literature as deliberate (Berlin, *Esther* JPS, 44–45; Sarna, *Genesis* JPS, 192; Levenson, *Esther* OTL, 78). The Esther echo is the load-bearing one: Mordecai's cry mirrors Esav's, marking Mordecai's situation as Esav-like and (in the lines of rabbinic tradition that read Haman as an Amalekite-Edomite descendant) closing a long-running narrative-arc. See [tzaaqah-gedolah-u-marah-bitter-cry](#tzaaqah-gedolah-u-marah-bitter-cry).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר בָּ֥א אָחִ֖יךָ בְּמִרְמָ֑ה וַיִּקַּ֖ח בִּרְכָתֶֽךָ׃

i18n.en: And he said, Your brother came with deceit, and has taken your blessing.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֡אמֶר הֲכִי֩ קָרָ֨א שְׁמ֜וֹ יַעֲקֹ֗ב וַֽיַּעְקְבֵ֙נִי֙ זֶ֣ה פַעֲמַ֔יִם אֶת־בְּכֹרָתִ֣י לָקָ֔ח וְהִנֵּ֥ה עַתָּ֖ה לָקַ֣ח בִּרְכָתִ֑י וַיֹּאמַ֕ר הֲלֹא־אָצַ֥לְתָּ לִּ֖י בְּרָכָֽה׃

i18n.en: And he said, Is he not rightly named Ya'aqov? For he has supplanted me these two times: he took my birthright, and behold, now he has taken my blessing. And he said, Have you not reserved a blessing for me?

paragraphs.commentary:
Esav's bitter pun on the *Ya'aqov / ʿqb* root. *Ha-khi qara shemo Ya'aqov va-y'aqveni zeh fa'amayim* — "is he not rightly named Ya'aqov, for he has supplanted me these two times?" The denominal verb *va-y'aqveni* (qal from the supplant / heel-trip root ʿqb) makes Esav's complaint the second of the two Ya'aqov-name-aetiologies in the patriarchal cycle — the first at Gen 25:26 (*v-yado ochezet ba-aqev*, his hand grasping the heel), the second here. Hosea 12:4 picks up the same etymology later as theological complaint. The standing entry [yaakov-name-etymology-aqev-supplant](#yaakov-name-etymology-aqev-supplant) supplies the lexical baseline and renders the verb "supplanted" per ASV; the literal heel-trip etymology is surfaced in the rationale rather than in the running text.

The *fa'amayim* ("two times") is enumerated in Esav's own next breath: *et-bekhorati laqach v-hineh atah laqach birkhati* — "he took my birthright, and behold, now he has taken my blessing." The pair *bekhorah / berakhah* is consonantally near-identical (ב־כ־ר / ב־ר־כ), transposing the middle radicals — a deliberate sound-play that marks the two losses as paired. The standing entry [bekhorah-birthright-firstborn-status](#bekhorah-birthright-firstborn-status) cross-references the Gen 25 birthright sale; the chapter's coda binds the two stories into a single Esav-loss narrative.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֨עַן יִצְחָ֜ק וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְעֵשָׂ֗ו הֵ֣ן גְּבִ֞יר שַׂמְתִּ֥יו לָךְ֙ וְאֶת־כָּל־אֶחָ֗יו נָתַ֤תִּי לוֹ֙ לַעֲבָדִ֔ים וְדָגָ֥ן וְתִירֹ֖שׁ סְמַכְתִּ֑יו וּלְכָ֣ה אֵפ֔וֹא מָ֥ה אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֖ה בְּנִֽי׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq answered and said to Esav, Behold, I have made him lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants; and with grain and new wine I have sustained him; and what then shall I do for you, my son?

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר עֵשָׂ֜ו אֶל־אָבִ֗יו הַֽבְרָכָ֨ה אַחַ֤ת הִֽוא־לְךָ֙ אָבִ֔י בָּרֲכֵ֥נִי גַם־אָ֖נִי אָבִ֑י וַיִּשָּׂ֥א עֵשָׂ֛ו קֹל֖וֹ וַיֵּֽבְךְּ׃

i18n.en: And Esav said to his father, Have you but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, my father. And Esav lifted up his voice, and wept.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֛עַן יִצְחָ֥ק אָבִ֖יו וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֑יו הִנֵּ֞ה מִשְׁמַנֵּ֤י הָאָ֙רֶץ֙ יִהְיֶ֣ה מֽוֹשָׁבֶ֔ךָ וּמִטַּ֥ל הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם מֵעָֽל׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq his father answered and said to him, Behold, away from the fatness of the land shall be your dwelling, and away from the dew of the skies from above.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The famous *mi-* ambiguity at the Esav counter-blessing.** *Hineh mi-shemanei ha-aretz yihye moshavekha u-mi-tal ha-shamayim me-al* — verbally near-identical to v 28's Ya'aqov-blessing but with the *mi-* preposition open to two diametrically opposite readings.

**Partitive reading** (ASV, KJV, rabbinic-harmonizing): "of the fatness of the land shall be your dwelling, and of the dew of the skies from above" — Esav receives a *parallel* blessing, sharing the same land-fertility and dew-from-above as Ya'aqov.

**Separative reading** (Westermann, *Genesis 12–36*; Speiser, *Genesis* AB; Sarna, *Genesis* JPS with discussion; NRSV; NJPS in its apparatus): "away from the fatness of the land shall be your dwelling, and away from the dew of the skies from above" — Esav is *exiled* from fertile-land and dew-region into desert-marginality, a reading that fits the geographical setting of the Edomite-Seir-mountain region (the southern desert-and-mountain Esav's descendants will inhabit, per Gen 36).

The two readings yield diametrically opposite blessings. The *mi-* preposition does both jobs in Biblical Hebrew, and the immediate context fixes neither: v 28's *mi-* is forced partitive by the parallel *v-rov dagan v-tirosh*, but v 39 lacks the disambiguating partitive parallel and the surrounding clauses (the sword-life and brother-service of v 40) lean separative.

**The Wheel of Heaven translation adopts the separative reading at the running text.** The context-favoring argument is decisive: Esav is being given the *lesser* blessing of the two; the partitive reading produces a near-duplicate of Ya'aqov's v 28 blessing, which loses the chapter's central irony (the stolen blessing was the inheritable one; Esav gets its inverse). The geographical reading — that Edomite territory is arid/marginal relative to Canaan — is supported by Gen 36's Edomite-genealogy and the *cherev tichye* ("by your sword you shall live") that follows immediately at v 40. Modern critical consensus (Westermann, Speiser, Sarna apparatus, NRSV) reads separative; ASV/KJV/NJPS main text preserve partitive. WoH chose with the modern critical consensus here over the older PD translation, departing from the *nivrakhu*-precedent because in this case modern critical scholarship is broadly aligned (not split as at Gen 12:3). See [mi-shemanei-ha-aretz-partitive-vs-separative](#mi-shemanei-ha-aretz-partitive-vs-separative).

paragraphs.text: וְעַל־חַרְבְּךָ֣ תִֽחְיֶ֔ה וְאֶת־אָחִ֖יךָ תַּעֲבֹ֑ד וְהָיָה֙ כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר תָּרִ֔יד וּפָרַקְתָּ֥ עֻלּ֖וֹ מֵעַ֥ל צַוָּארֶֽךָ׃

i18n.en: And by your sword shall you live, and your brother shall you serve; and it shall come to pass, when you break loose, that you shall break his yoke from off your neck.

paragraphs.commentary:
Two clauses, both load-bearing for the Edomite-tradition setup.

*V-al-charbekha tichye v-et achikha ta'avod* — "by your sword shall you live, and your brother shall you serve." The sword-and-service couplet is the structural opposite of Ya'aqov's *g'vir l-acheikha* ("lord over your brothers") at v 29. The pair marks Esav / Edom as the warrior-vassal foil to Ya'aqov / Israel — a typology developed across the corpus (2 Kgs 8:20–22 on Edom's revolt under Yehoram; Mal 1:2–5 "Esav I hated"; Obadiah's entire 21-verse oracle against Edom; 1 Macc 5:3 on Judah's campaign against the Idumeans).

*V-haya ka-asher tarid u-faraqta ulo me-al tzavarekha* — "and it shall come to pass, when you break loose, that you shall break his yoke from off your neck." The verb *tarid* (תָּרִיד) is cognate-difficult: possibly (a) from *rud* — "wander, rove, become restless" (ASV's "when thou shalt break loose"), (b) linked to *radah* — "rule" (some medieval Jewish exegesis, KJV-Targum "have the dominion"), or (c) an alternative philological reconstruction toward "grow aggrieved" (NJPS "when you grow restive"). The translation follows ASV's *break loose* per the project's ASV-baseline convention. The clause is the prophetic counterpart to the v 39 blessing-ambiguity: Esav serves Ya'aqov for a time, then throws off the yoke — historically realized in the 2 Kgs 8 Edomite revolt and developed in the Edom-typology through Obadiah and the Hasmonean period. See [cherev-tichye-by-the-sword-edom-tradition](#cherev-tichye-by-the-sword-edom-tradition).

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׂטֹ֤ם עֵשָׂו֙ אֶֽת־יַעֲקֹ֔ב עַל־הַ֨בְּרָכָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בֵּרֲכ֖וֹ אָבִ֑יו וַיֹּ֨אמֶר עֵשָׂ֜ו בְּלִבּ֗וֹ יִקְרְבוּ֙ יְמֵי֙ אֵ֣בֶל אָבִ֔י וְאַֽהַרְגָ֖ה אֶת־יַעֲקֹ֥ב אָחִֽי׃

i18n.en: And Esav hated Ya'aqov on account of the blessing with which his father had blessed him; and Esav said in his heart, The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill Ya'aqov my brother.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yistom Esav et-Ya'aqov* — "and Esav hated Ya'aqov." The verb *satam* (שָׂטַם) is a near-synonym of the standard *sane* (שָׂנֵא, "hate") but with the distinctive nuance of "bear a grudge, harbor sustained resentment, lie in wait for" (BDB 966; HALOT s.v.). The cross-corpus distribution (Gen 49:23 of Joseph's brothers; 50:15 again of Joseph's brothers; Job 16:9 and 30:21 of God; Ps 55:4) supports the sustained-grudge / ambush-readiness reading rather than the flat-hate of *sane*.

The verb-choice is plausibly editorial: it foreshadows the explicit kill-plan in the verse's continuation (*v-aharga et-Ya'aqov achi*, "then I will kill Ya'aqov my brother"). ASV's flat "hated" is preserved as the running translation, but the nuance is the satam-grudge, not the sane-hatred. The chapter's last hostile word before Ya'aqov's twenty-year exile is lexically the grudge-verb, not the hate-verb — a calibration the narrator makes deliberately.

paragraphs.text: וַיֻּגַּ֣ד לְרִבְקָ֔ה אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֥י עֵשָׂ֖ו בְּנָ֣הּ הַגָּדֹ֑ל וַתִּשְׁלַ֞ח וַתִּקְרָ֤א לְיַעֲקֹב֙ בְּנָ֣הּ הַקָּטָ֔ן וַתֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו הִנֵּה֙ עֵשָׂ֣ו אָחִ֔יךָ מִתְנַחֵ֥ם לְךָ֖ לְהָרְגֶֽךָ׃

i18n.en: And the words of Esav her elder son were told to Rivkah; and she sent and called Ya'aqov her younger son, and said to him, Behold, your brother Esav is consoling himself concerning you, by planning to kill you.

paragraphs.text: וְעַתָּ֥ה בְנִ֖י שְׁמַ֣ע בְּקֹלִ֑י וְק֧וּם בְּרַח־לְךָ֛ אֶל־לָבָ֥ן אָחִ֖י חָרָֽנָה׃

i18n.en: Now therefore, my son, obey my voice; and arise, flee to Lavan my brother, to Haran;

paragraphs.text: וְיָשַׁבְתָּ֥ עִמּ֖וֹ יָמִ֣ים אֲחָדִ֑ים עַ֥ד אֲשֶׁר־תָּשׁ֖וּב חֲמַ֥ת אָחִֽיךָ׃

i18n.en: And dwell with him a few days, until your brother's fury turns away;

paragraphs.text: עַד־שׁ֨וּב אַף־אָחִ֜יךָ מִמְּךָ֗ וְשָׁכַח֙ אֵ֣ת אֲשֶׁר־עָשִׂ֣יתָ לּ֔וֹ וְשָׁלַחְתִּ֖י וּלְקַחְתִּ֣יךָ מִשָּׁ֑ם לָמָ֥ה אֶשְׁכַּ֛ל גַּם־שְׁנֵיכֶ֖ם י֥וֹם אֶחָֽד׃

i18n.en: Until your brother's anger turns away from you, and he forgets what you have done to him; then I will send and fetch you from there. Why should I be bereaved of you both in one day?

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר רִבְקָה֙ אֶל־יִצְחָ֔ק קַ֣צְתִּי בְחַיַּ֔י מִפְּנֵ֖י בְּנ֣וֹת חֵ֑ת אִם־לֹקֵ֣חַ יַ֠עֲקֹב אִשָּׁ֨ה מִבְּנֽוֹת־חֵ֤ת כָּאֵ֙לֶּה֙ מִבְּנ֣וֹת הָאָ֔רֶץ לָ֥מָּה לִּ֖י חַיִּֽים׃

i18n.en: And Rivkah said to Yitzchaq, I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Het; if Ya'aqov takes a wife of the daughters of Het, such as these, of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life be to me?

paragraphs.commentary:
*Qatzti b-chayyai mi-p'nei b'not Chet* — "I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Het." Rivkah's closing speech recycles the Hittite-wives complaint from Gen 26:34–35 (Esav's marriage to Yehudit bat-Be'eri and Basemat bat-Elon, *morat ruach* to Yitzchaq and Rivkah — see [morat-ruach-bitterness-of-spirit-esau-hittite-wives](#morat-ruach-bitterness-of-spirit-esau-hittite-wives)) and deploys it as the **pretext** for her recommendation that Ya'aqov be sent away to Lavan in Aram-Naharaim.

The narrative-logical relationship is editorially load-bearing. The *real* reason for Ya'aqov's departure — Esav's death-threat at vv 41–45 — is told only to Rivkah and Ya'aqov; Yitzchaq is not informed. What Rivkah brings to Yitzchaq at v 46 is a *decoy reason*, a topic she knows he shares concern about (per Gen 26:35), so the dispatch reads to Yitzchaq as bride-search rather than as flight. The rhetorical-cover is one of the chapter's most-studied narrative-strategic moves (Alter, *The Art of Biblical Narrative* ch. 6 on information-asymmetry in the Genesis narrator; Sternberg, *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* on multi-layered dialogue-pragmatics).

The Wheel of Heaven lens reads the chapter as already showing what the rest of the corpus will repeatedly model: human characters operate the larger plan through partial knowledge, pretexts, and information-asymmetry, not through transparent shared deliberation. Rivkah's pretext is not a flaw in the narrative — it is the narrative's working assumption about how providential outcomes get realized through ordinary human cunning. See [rebekah-pretext-hittite-wives-cover](#rebekah-pretext-hittite-wives-cover).
